newsitem.title: GERMANY: Stealthy Berlin commandos thwart Bosnian hijacker.
newsitem.headline: Stealthy Berlin commandos thwart Bosnian hijacker.

text.p: A knife-wielding Bosnian refugee facing deportation hijacked an Austrian Airlines plane on Tuesday but was disarmed by Berlin police commandos who secretly boarded the plane and pushed him out of an open door.

Police in Berlin said the 39-year-old Bosnian man, whose permit to live in Germany was set to expire next Tuesday, fell about seven metres (yards) to the tarmac at Berlin's Tegel airport, where he was quickly overpowered and arrested.
None of the passengers or crew was hurt.
"Two officers entered from the rear of the plane and the perpetrator was standing in an open door at the front," said Bernd Meyer, a Berlin police spokesman at a news conference.
"They stormed to the front and one of the officers was able to push him out of the open door."
The hijacker was charged with kidnapping and air piracy, police said. He could face up to 15 years in jail if convicted.

Meyer declined to say how the man had managed to get the knife and a baton onto the plane. Security at the west Berlin airport has been thorough since the Cold War era. It includes body searches of all passengers boarding aircraft.

The Bosnian, who police said smelled strongly of alcohol, seized the Austrian Airlines flight with 28 passengers and five crew from Berlin at around noon as the plane was beginning its approach to Vienna airport.

After pulling out a 25 cm (10 inch) long knife and a 35 cm (14 inch) baton, the Bosnian stormed to the front of the aircraft and into the cockpit. He told the pilot his demands were a residency and work permit in Germany, authorities said.

The plane, a McDonnell-Douglas MD-80, was only one-quarter full. It returned to Berlin and was parked in an isolated area of the airport, where negotiations were set to start. The passengers included Germans, Austrians and Japanese.
A translator and police were preparing to negotiate with the hijacker when the commandos struck.
"It never got that far because a police special unit overpowered the assailant and quickly arrested him," said Ruediger Reiff, spokesman for Berlin's justice ministry.
Walter Bock, a chief pilot for Austrian Airlines in Vienna, was in radio contact with the plane, which he said was flying over Prague when the hijacker stormed into the cockpit.
He said he was carrying a knife and a bat and demanded the plane be turned back to Berlin.
Airline officials said the plane had been carrying enough fuel for the return flight. It was the first time in Austrian Airlines' history that a plane has been hijacked.

Berlin airport authorities said there were no air traffic delays. The airport in western Berlin is the busiest of three airports in Germany's new capital, but its air traffic is dwarfed by Frankfurt's international airport.
Reiff said the Bosnian, who was only identified by the initial L, had been living in northern Germany. They said he was not a resident of Berlin and had no police record.
There are about 320,000 Bosnian refugees in Germany. Several German states have recently begun the forced repatration of Bosnians now that the 43-month-long war there has ended.

The hijacking was similar to a 1994 attack by a Bosnian Moslem named Haris Kec, who commandeered a domestic Scandinavian Airlines System plane with 116 passengers and six crew after takeoff from Bardufoss inside the Arctic circle.
Saying he had bombs and hand grenades, the hijacker threatened to blow up the plane unless Norway took the lead in international efforts to provide food for war-battered Bosnia.
Kec surrendered at Oslo's Gardermoen airport. Nobody was injured and it turned out he had been unarmed.
